name: Automation and Controller-Based Networking
author: Recurse
subject: networking
description: How automation and controllers change network management: planes, APIs, ACI, SD-Access, SD-WAN and cloud dashboards.

lesson.intro: Engineers used to configure networks one box at a time. Controllers, APIs and automation let you describe what the network should do once and have software make every device do it. This is the mental model CCNA domain 6 tests.
objectives: Classify device work into the data, control and management planes
Compare traditional networking with controller-based networking and automation
Identify northbound and southbound APIs, NETCONF, RESTCONF and YANG
Describe the underlay, overlay and fabric of SD-Access and SD-WAN
Explain what Catalyst Center and cloud dashboards add, and what survives a controller outage

sections.title: What automation changes
sections.key: Automation applies one definition of a change to every device, which brings consistency, speed, scale and fewer errors, and lets tools catch configuration drift.
sections.body:
Monday's request: add an NTP server, a syslog server and one ACL line to 400 branch switches. By hand, at three minutes a switch, that is 20 hours of typing, and around switch 250 someone pastes into the wrong window.

**Network automation** has software apply one definition of the change to all 400.

[[visual]]

**Configuration drift** is a device slowly diverging from others in the same role, usually through one-off manual fixes. A good tool compares each device with the intended configuration and reports both missing and extra lines.

[[visual 2]]

[[visual 3]]

Programs need **structured data**. Scraping `show` output breaks when a release moves a column or rewords a line; an API returns the same facts as named fields from a defined data model.

[[visual 4]]

visual.title: What automation improves
rows: Every device gets the same lines: no snowflakes (one-off devices nobody understands)
Days of changes run in minutes; new devices come up configured on day 0
No typos or skipped devices; changes validated before and after
10 devices or 1,000 take about the same effort
Tools compare devices with the intended configuration and fix differences
Changes live in version control: who, what, when and why

items.title: Configuration management
points: Provisioning new settings, such as an ACL line on 300 routers
Enforcing the standard for each role

items.title: Operational management
points: Spotting an uplink whose use keeps climbing
Checking every device runs an approved software image

steps.label: Day 0: onboard it (Plug and Play, zero-touch)
Day 1: apply the standard configuration for its role
Day n: monitor, patch and change it for years
Retire: decommission and remove from inventory

visual.title: One port's trunking state, two ways

sections.deeper:
Automation does not replace networking knowledge. A script pushes exactly what you told it to, including your mistakes, to every device at once, so the engineer still has to know what correct looks like.

The day 0, day 1 and day n vocabulary comes from operations teams in general, not only networking. Day 0 is everything up to the device being reachable and managed, day 1 makes it do its job, and day n is the long tail of upgrades, fixes and changes until it is replaced.
sections.tip: When the exam asks what automation improves, think consistency, speed, scale and fewer human errors.
sections.pitfall: Automation multiplies mistakes as efficiently as good changes. Test in a lab, do a dry run, then roll out to a small group of devices before the rest.

check.question: A team finds that 14 of its 300 branch routers have slightly different QoS settings from the rest, all caused by one-off fixes made during outages. What is this called, and what helps most?
choices: Route flapping; a routing protocol with faster timers
Control plane failure; moving routing into a controller
Configuration drift; a tool that compares devices with the intended configuration
Configuration drift; a longer weekly change approval meeting
check.explanation: Devices of the same role slowly diverging through manual one-off changes is configuration drift. A configuration management tool that compares each device with the intended configuration finds and fixes it. More meetings do not show you which devices already differ.

sections.title: Data, control and management planes
sections.key: The data plane forwards each message, the control plane builds the tables it uses, and the management plane lets people and tools manage the device.
sections.body:
Follow one packet through a router. It arrives on G0/0, matches the routing table and leaves G0/1 with a new Ethernet header. OSPF filled that table long before, and meanwhile an engineer reads the configuration over SSH. Three kinds of work, and software-defined networking is built on telling them apart.

[[visual]]

Quick test: work done to each packet or frame is data plane; work that fills or changes a table is control plane; work that lets someone manage the box is management plane. A router with SSH disabled still routes.

[[visual 2]]

In a traditional network every device has all three planes, and the control plane is **distributed**: each router runs its own OSPF and makes its own decisions.

items.title: Data plane
points: Acts on each message as it passes
NAT rewrites, ACL and port security discards

items.title: Management plane
points: APIs such as NETCONF and RESTCONF

visual.title: Inside a switch

layers.label: CPU running IOS
layers.detail: most control and management plane work

layers.label: ASIC with TCAM
layers.detail: data plane: millions of frames per second

visual.caption: An **ASIC** (application-specific integrated circuit) forwards in hardware, and **TCAM** (ternary content-addressable memory) returns the matching table entry in one lookup instead of a search.

sections.tip: Exam hook: the control plane decides, the data plane does, and the management plane lets you manage.
sections.pitfall: Classify by what the work does, not where it runs. MAC learning is control plane because it builds the MAC table. You configure an ACL through the management plane, but discarding a packet is data plane.

check.question: A switch adds an 802.1Q header to a frame before sending it out a trunk. Which plane is doing this work?
choices: Control plane
Data plane
Management plane
Policy plane
check.explanation: Tagging happens to each frame as it is forwarded, so it is data plane work. The control plane builds tables (routing, MAC, STP state); it does not touch each frame.

sections.title: Traditional versus controller-based networking
sections.key: A controller centralizes some of the network's work so you configure the network once instead of each device, and it is not in the forwarding path.
sections.body:
In a traditional network each router runs its own routing protocol, each switch its own STP, and an engineer configures every device through its own CLI. It is resilient, but every change is a per-device job and nobody has one live view.

A **controller** is software on a server, VM or appliance that learns every device, the topology and the configuration, and becomes the place where people and programs operate the network. This is **software-defined networking (SDN)**, also called controller-based networking or software-defined architecture.

[[visual]]

The trade-offs:

- The controller becomes critical infrastructure that must be highly available, secured and licensed.
- The team needs new skills, and features depend on supported hardware.

[[visual 2]]

visual.title: What changes
rows: Each device, one at a time
The controller, once for the network
Central data that analytics and AI can mine

visual.title: The controller sits beside the traffic
visual.caption: If Catalyst Center or the ACI controller goes offline, devices keep forwarding with the configuration and tables they have. You lose changes and the network-wide view until it returns.

sections.tip: Look for "configure the network rather than each device" in exam answers. It is the core advantage of controller-based networking.
sections.pitfall: Controller-based does not mean the controller is in the forwarding path. User traffic never passes through it; if it fails you lose changes and visibility, not connectivity.

check.question: What is the core change in how engineers work when a campus moves from traditional to controller-based networking?
choices: Every device must still be configured from its own CLI, just faster
Engineers define policy once on the controller, which configures every device consistently through southbound interfaces
User traffic is forwarded through the controller so it can enforce policy
Devices stop running any control plane protocols at all
check.explanation: Controller-based networking moves the engineer from configuring devices to configuring the network: one policy on the controller, pushed consistently to devices. Traffic still flows device to device, and in most designs the devices keep much of their control plane.

sections.title: Three ways to split the planes
sections.key: Controllers centralize different amounts: OpenFlow most of the control plane, ACI policy pushed to a spine-leaf fabric, and Catalyst Center managing ordinary devices none of it.
sections.body:
Every SDN design moves some work into a controller. How much varies, and the exam tests the difference.

[[visual]]

**OpenFlow**, defined by the Open Networking Foundation (ONF), lets a controller such as **OpenDaylight** write match-and-action entries straight into switch flow tables. It is the textbook separation of control and data planes.

**Cisco ACI** (Application Centric Infrastructure) runs on Nexus 9000 switches in a **spine-leaf** data center fabric:

[[visual 2]]

In ACI you define **endpoint groups** (EPGs, such as Web, App and DB) and contracts saying which may talk. The **APIC** pushes them with **OpFlex**. Policy follows the EPG, not the port: when a VM moves to another leaf, the APIC programs that leaf.

**Management-plane controllers** like Catalyst Center configure devices that still run their own STP, MAC learning and routing. Most enterprises start here.

rows: Stays and works out the details of the policy

visual.title: Spine-leaf
visual.caption: Every leaf links to every spine. No leaf-to-leaf or spine-to-spine links. Endpoints, including the APIC and WAN routers, attach only to leaves, so traffic between leaves always goes leaf, spine, leaf.

sections.tip: Spine-leaf in one line: leaves connect to every spine, spines connect only to leaves, and endpoints live on leaves.
sections.pitfall: Do not assume every controller removes the control plane from devices. Only OpenFlow centralizes most of it; Catalyst Center managing traditional devices leaves their control plane exactly as it was.

check.question: Which statement correctly compares OpenFlow-based SDN with Catalyst Center managing traditional switches?
choices: OpenFlow centralizes most control plane work, while Catalyst Center leaves the switches' control plane in place and configures them
Both remove the control plane from every switch and program flows directly
Catalyst Center centralizes the data plane, while OpenFlow centralizes only management
Neither changes how devices are configured; both only draw topology maps
check.explanation: In the OpenFlow model the controller programs forwarding entries into switches, so most control plane work is centralized. Catalyst Center managing ordinary devices changes their configuration through the management plane, but the devices still run their own routing, STP and MAC learning.

sections.title: Northbound and southbound APIs
sections.key: The northbound API faces up to apps and scripts, usually REST with JSON; southbound interfaces face down to devices: OpenFlow, OpFlex, NETCONF, RESTCONF, SSH and SNMP.
sections.body:
Draw the controller in the middle of a page: devices below, and the GUI, Python scripts, Ansible and ticketing apps above. Each direction is named for where it sits.

[[visual]]

An **API** (application programming interface) is a defined way for one program to exchange data with another. A northbound API is valuable for the work the controller does for you: one path trace request returns the hops, interfaces and ACLs, instead of you pulling tables from dozens of devices.

Modern southbound options are **model-driven**. **YANG** is a data modeling language: a YANG model defines which configuration and state data exist (an interface's name, description, enabled state, addresses), with names and types.

[[visual 2]]

The explorer below holds a real northbound reply: named fields, not text to scrape.

layers.label: Northbound API (NBI)
layers.detail: REST over HTTPS with JSON; Catalyst Center calls it the Intent API

layers.label: Southbound (SBI)
layers.detail: OpenFlow, OpFlex, NETCONF, RESTCONF, SSH or Telnet CLI, SNMP

visual.title: Southbound options
rows: Writes match and action entries into switch flow tables
Carries Cisco ACI policy from the APIC to the switches
YANG data as XML operations (get-config, edit-config) over SSH, TCP port 830; can validate a whole change before committing. Enable with `netconf-yang`
YANG data through REST-style HTTPS URIs, as JSON or XML. Enable with `ip http secure-server` and `restconf`
The classics: CLI commands, and polling or setting MIB values

sections.tip: Northbound points up to apps and scripts; southbound points down to devices, exactly as they sit on the drawing.
sections.pitfall: Direction is about who talks to whom, not the protocol name. A script calling the controller's REST API is northbound. The controller configuring a switch with RESTCONF is southbound, despite the REST in its name.

activity.title: What a northbound API returns
activity.prompt: This is a trimmed reply from Catalyst Center to GET /dna/intent/api/v1/network-device. Find the role of the second device and the software version both devices run. Then look closely: interfaceCount is a quoted string, not a number, and location is null. A script reads these as named values instead of scraping show output.

check.question: A Python script on an engineer's laptop asks Catalyst Center for every switch running an old software version. Which interface does the script use?
choices: The southbound interface, using NETCONF
The southbound interface, using OpenFlow
The management plane of each switch, using SNMP
The northbound interface, using a REST API
check.explanation: Applications and scripts talk to the controller through its northbound interface, which on Catalyst Center is a REST API. The controller then uses its southbound interfaces to collect data from the switches.

sections.title: Underlay, overlay and fabric: SD-Access
sections.key: In SD-Access the underlay gives fabric nodes IP reachability, the overlay carries endpoint traffic in VXLAN tunnels, and the fabric is the two together.
sections.body:
Cisco **Software-Defined Access** (SD-Access or SDA) is the controller-based campus design, with Catalyst Center as its controller.

[[visual]]

On new hardware Catalyst Center builds a **routed access** underlay: every switch is Layer 3, every inter-switch link is routed, and they run **IS-IS**. With no Layer 2 links between switches STP has nothing to block, and the edge node is the hosts' default gateway, so no HSRP is needed.

In the overlay, **LISP** is the control plane and **VXLAN** the data plane. Each edge node registers its endpoint IDs (**EIDs**, endpoint addresses) with its own **RLOC** (routing locator, its underlay address):

[[visual 2]]

[[visual 3]]

The VXLAN header carries a **scalable group tag (SGT)**. Cisco ISE puts each user or device in a group, and policy says which groups may talk, so security follows the user, not the IP address.

rows: Physical switches, links and routing that give every fabric node IP reachability
Virtual networks carried in VXLAN tunnels between fabric nodes
Underlay plus overlay: the complete system
Connects endpoints, like an access switch
Connects the fabric to outside networks, such as the WAN or a data center
Runs the LISP map server: where every endpoint lives

visual.title: First frame to a new destination

messages.note: A frame for 10.1.3.1 arrives from PC 10.1.1.1

visual.title: What crosses the underlay
visual.caption: Underlay switches route on the outer header only. The inner frame keeps the endpoints' own addresses. VXLAN runs in the switch ASICs, so it costs no forwarding speed.

sections.deeper:
On existing production gear (brownfield), engineers usually configure the underlay themselves so the controller does not disrupt live traffic, and Catalyst Center then builds the overlay on top.

The VNI (VXLAN network identifier) in the header says which virtual network the frame belongs to, so one fabric can keep separate virtual networks apart, much like VRFs.
sections.tip: Memory hook: the underlay is underneath (links and IP reachability), the overlay is laid over it (tunnels), and the fabric is both.
sections.pitfall: The outer IP header uses underlay addresses (RLOCs); the inner packet keeps the endpoints' addresses. And keep the overlay planes straight: LISP is control plane, VXLAN is data plane.

check.question: In SD-Access, which statement correctly describes the underlay?
choices: VXLAN tunnels that carry endpoint traffic between fabric edge nodes
The LISP database that maps endpoint IDs to routing locators
The scalable group policy matrix stored on Catalyst Center
The physical devices, links and routing that give fabric nodes IP reachability to each other
check.explanation: The underlay is the physical network plus its routing (IS-IS in a greenfield fabric), there so fabric nodes can reach each other. VXLAN tunnels are the overlay, and LISP is the overlay's control plane.

sections.title: SD-WAN: an overlay across any transport
sections.key: SD-WAN builds IPsec tunnels across any transport, with separate parts for management (Manager), control (Controller, running OMP), onboarding (Validator) and forwarding (edge routers).
sections.body:
A retailer has 600 stores, each with an expensive MPLS circuit and an idle broadband backup, and every policy change touches 600 routers. **SD-WAN** (software-defined WAN) fixes both.

[[visual]]

Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN (originally Viptela) gives each plane its own component. Cisco renamed them in 2023, and study material uses both names:

[[visual 2]]

With every path in view, the controllers push **application-aware routing**: edge routers measure loss, latency and jitter on every tunnel with **BFD** probes and send each application over a path that meets its SLA.

[[visual 3]]

New sites use **zero-touch provisioning**: the router contacts the Validator, authenticates, and downloads its configuration from the Manager. If the controllers become unreachable, edge routers keep forwarding over existing tunnels with the routes and keys they last received, for a graceful restart period.

visual.caption: The **underlay** is any transport with IP reachability: MPLS, broadband internet, 4G or 5G. The **overlay** is a mesh of **IPsec** tunnels between edge routers across every transport, encrypted even over the internet.

rows: GUI, templates, policy, monitoring and the northbound REST API
Runs **OMP** (Overlay Management Protocol) with every edge: routes, keys and policy. Edges never swap routes directly
First contact: authenticates new routers, tells them where the controllers are, helps with NAT traversal
Forward user traffic through the tunnels

visual.title: Store17: where does voice go?
visual.caption: Voice SLA: latency under 150 ms, loss under 1%, jitter under 30 ms. The path that meets every limit wins, whatever the transport.

sections.tip: Match each name to its plane: the Manager manages, the Controller controls (OMP), the Validator validates new routers, and edge routers forward.
sections.pitfall: The SD-WAN underlay is not just MPLS. Any transport that gives IP reachability, including the public internet and cellular, is underlay; the IPsec tunnels across them are the overlay.

check.question: In Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN, which component runs OMP and distributes routes and policy to the edge routers?
choices: SD-WAN Manager (vManage)
SD-WAN Validator (vBond)
SD-WAN Controller (vSmart)
The WAN Edge router at headquarters
check.explanation: The SD-WAN Controller is the control plane: it runs OMP with every edge router. The Manager is the management plane GUI and API, the Validator onboards and authenticates routers, and edge routers forward traffic.

sections.title: Catalyst Center and intent-based networking
sections.key: Catalyst Center (formerly DNA Center) does what traditional management platforms do, and adds SD-Access, intent-based group policy, assurance and a northbound REST API.
sections.body:
Cisco DNA Center was renamed **Catalyst Center** in 2023, and you will see both names. It controls SD-Access fabrics and also manages ordinary, non-fabric networks.

[[visual]]

**Intent-based networking (IBN)** is the idea underneath. You state the outcome, such as "guests reach the internet but nothing internal", and the controller translates it into device configuration, deploys it and keeps checking that the network behaves that way.

Compare a traditional ACL that has grown for years: nobody dares delete a line, because nobody knows which old requirement it serves. Group-based policy keeps each rule as a separate cell with its reason, so you can remove one without touching the others.

[[visual 2]]

items.title: Both
items.sub: traditional tools such as Prime Infrastructure, and Catalyst Center
points: Discovery, inventory and topology maps (SNMP, SSH, CDP, LLDP)
Day 0, day 1 and day n lifecycle
Plug and Play for new devices

items.title: Only Catalyst Center
points: Intent-based group policy instead of interface ACLs
Assurance: Device 360, Client 360, AI baselines, network time travel
Path trace, including ACLs along the path
QoS deployed from a few application policy choices
Northbound REST API; SSH, SNMP, NETCONF, RESTCONF southbound

visual.title: Group-based policy (source down, destination across)
visual.caption: No IP addresses and no interface ACLs: ISE puts each user in a group, and the fabric enforces the cell for each source and destination group.

sections.tip: If an answer says the engineer configures the network as a whole, by intent or policy, rather than device by device, it describes controller-based management.
sections.pitfall: Catalyst Center does not make traditional features disappear. Discovery, topology maps and day 0, 1 and n lifecycle work are shared with traditional tools; SD-Access and intent-based policy set it apart.

check.question: Which capability belongs to Catalyst Center but not to a traditional network management platform?
choices: Discovering devices and drawing a topology map
Building and controlling an SD-Access fabric with group-based policy
Polling interface counters with SNMP
Backing up device configurations on a schedule
check.explanation: Traditional platforms also discover devices, poll with SNMP and back up configurations. Running an SD-Access fabric with intent-based group policy is what Catalyst Center adds.

sections.title: Cloud-managed networks
sections.key: In a cloud-managed network the management plane lives in the vendor's cloud while user traffic stays local, so devices keep forwarding if the cloud is unreachable.
sections.body:
A coffee chain opens 40 stores a year with no IT staff. The store manager plugs in a switch and an access point, and minutes later they appear on a dashboard at headquarters. That is **cloud-managed networking**: Cisco Meraki, and cloud-managed Catalyst gear.

[[visual]]

- **Only management traffic** goes to the cloud: configuration, firmware and health data. User traffic is forwarded locally.
- **Zero-touch provisioning**: claim devices by serial or order number, and they configure themselves on first contact.
- **Cloud unreachable**: devices keep forwarding with their last configuration; you lose the dashboard and changes.
- One dashboard for every site, a northbound REST API, and no controller hardware to patch.

The trade-offs: subscription licensing that must stay current, management that depends on internet access, and network data held by a third party (privacy and data residency).

[[visual 2]]

visual.caption: User traffic stays local. Each device keeps an outbound, encrypted connection to the cloud, which pushes configuration and firmware and collects statistics.

visual.title: Three management models
visual.caption: In all three, user traffic stays local.

sections.tip: Cloud-managed means the management plane lives in the cloud while the data plane stays on site.
sections.pitfall: A tempting wrong answer says cloud-managed networks send all user traffic through the cloud. They do not; only management and telemetry traffic goes there.

check.question: A branch with cloud-managed switches loses its internet connection for an hour. What happens to traffic between two PCs in that branch?
choices: It stops, because the switches need the cloud to make forwarding decisions
It is redirected through the vendor's nearest data center over a backup tunnel
It keeps flowing locally; only management from the dashboard is unavailable
It keeps flowing, but every switch reboots into a factory default configuration
check.explanation: Cloud management moves the management plane to the cloud, not the data plane. Local switching keeps working with the last configuration; you just cannot see or change the devices until the cloud is reachable again.

keyTerms.definition: Per-message forwarding work: table lookups, encapsulation, tagging, NAT and ACL filtering. Also called the forwarding plane.
Work that builds the tables the data plane uses, such as routing protocols, ARP, MAC learning and STP.
Protocols used to manage a device, such as SSH, SNMP, syslog and NETCONF.
Software that centralizes some control or management functions and exposes the network to people and programs.
The interface from a controller up to applications and scripts, usually a REST API returning JSON.
The interface from a controller down to devices, such as OpenFlow, OpFlex, NETCONF, RESTCONF, SSH and SNMP.
The physical network and its routing, which give fabric nodes IP reachability to each other.
Virtual networks built on the underlay with tunnels; in SD-Access, VXLAN tunnels between fabric nodes.
The underlay and overlay together, managed as one system.
Stating the desired outcome and letting the controller translate it into configuration and verify the result.
A device's configuration diverging over time from others in the same role, usually through one-off manual changes.
Devices managed from a vendor-hosted dashboard; only management traffic goes to the cloud.
An ONF southbound protocol a controller uses to write match and action entries directly into switch flow tables.
A data center topology where every leaf connects to every spine, endpoints attach only to leaves, and there are no leaf-leaf or spine-spine links.
The ACI controller, and the endpoint groups whose policies it pushes to the switches with OpFlex.
A data modeling language that defines the names, types and structure of device data carried by NETCONF and RESTCONF.
Model-driven management protocols: NETCONF uses XML over SSH on port 830, RESTCONF uses HTTPS with JSON or XML.
A controller-based WAN that builds an IPsec overlay across any transport and steers applications by measured path quality.
Overlay Management Protocol: the SD-WAN control plane protocol between the SD-WAN Controller and edge routers.

summary: Automation brings consistency, speed, scale and fewer errors, and catches configuration drift.
Data plane forwards, control plane builds the tables, management plane lets you manage.
OpenFlow centralizes most control work, ACI pushes policy with OpFlex, Catalyst Center manages ordinary devices.
Northbound APIs (REST, JSON) face apps; southbound (OpenFlow, OpFlex, NETCONF, RESTCONF, SSH, SNMP) face devices.
Underlay gives reachability, overlay tunnels across it: VXLAN with LISP in SD-Access, IPsec with OMP in SD-WAN.
Controllers are not in the forwarding path: if they fail, devices keep forwarding.
lesson.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a new network technician what changes when a company moves from configuring each switch and router by hand to Catalyst Center with SD-Access and Cisco SD-WAN. Cover the three planes, northbound and southbound APIs, what the underlay and overlay each do, and what happens if the controllers go offline.

questions.question: A Layer 2 switch looks up a frame's destination MAC address and forwards it out G0/2 only. Which plane does this work belong to?
choices: Control plane
Management plane
Data plane
Southbound plane
questions.explanation: Forwarding each frame by matching the MAC table is data plane work. The control plane built that table (MAC learning), but using it to forward is the data plane.

questions.question: A router learns a route from an OSPF neighbor and installs it in its routing table. Which plane is this?
choices: Data plane
Control plane
Management plane
Forwarding plane
questions.explanation: Routing protocols build the tables the data plane uses, which is control plane work. Forwarding plane is another name for the data plane, so it is wrong here.

questions.question: Match each task to the plane it belongs to.

pairs.left: NAT rewrites a packet's source address
pairs.right: Data plane

pairs.left: STP moves a port to the blocking state
pairs.right: Control plane

pairs.left: An SNMP manager polls interface counters
pairs.right: Management plane

questions.explanation: NAT acts on each packet (data plane). STP decides which ports may forward, shaping the data plane's behavior (control plane). SNMP exists so tools can monitor and manage the device (management plane).

questions.question: Which two of these are control plane functions? Choose two.
choices: ARP resolving a next-hop MAC address
An ACL discarding a packet
A switch learning source MAC addresses
Encrypting a packet for a site-to-site VPN
An engineer connecting with SSH
questions.explanation: ARP and MAC learning both build tables the data plane uses, so they are control plane. ACL filtering and VPN encryption act on each packet (data plane), and SSH is management plane.

questions.question: Why do switches forward frames with an ASIC and TCAM instead of the general-purpose CPU?
choices: The CPU cannot run routing protocols or STP
TCAM stores the startup-config so it survives a reload
Forwarding millions of frames per second needs hardware lookups a CPU running software cannot match
The ASIC encrypts management traffic such as SSH and SNMPv3
questions.explanation: Even a small switch must forward millions of frames per second, so the data plane runs in purpose-built hardware: the ASIC does the forwarding and TCAM returns a table match in a single lookup. The CPU runs IOS and most control and management plane work.

questions.question: Which statement best describes configuration drift?
choices: A device's configuration changing over time so that it differs from other devices in the same role
A device's running-config being larger than its startup-config
Routes appearing and disappearing from the routing table
A device losing its configuration after a power failure
questions.explanation: Drift is gradual divergence from the standard for a role, usually caused by one-off manual changes. Automation tools detect it by comparing devices with the intended configuration.

questions.question: An automation script must find the operational trunking state of every port on 600 switches. Why is reading it from an API with a defined data model better than parsing the show command output?
choices: The API makes the switches forward frames faster
Show commands cannot be run over SSH by a script
The API removes the need to understand trunking
The API returns named fields, so the script does not break when the CLI output format changes
questions.explanation: Screen scraping depends on the exact layout of human-readable text, which changes between releases and platforms. A data model gives each fact a stable name and type that programs can read directly.

questions.question: An automation tool pushes a change with a template error, and OSPF breaks on all 300 branch routers at once. Which practice would most directly have limited the damage?
choices: Configuring each router by hand instead
Testing in a lab and rolling the change out to a small group of devices first
Disabling SSH on the routers so the tool cannot connect
Running the tool more often so it repairs itself
questions.explanation: Automation applies mistakes at scale just as well as good changes. Testing first and rolling out in stages (a pilot group, then the rest) keeps one bad change from reaching everything at once, while keeping the benefits of automation.

questions.question: Which two are advantages of controller-based networking compared with traditional networking? Choose two.
choices: Configuring features for the network as a whole instead of per device
Every device keeps fully independent forwarding decisions
More consistent device configuration with fewer errors
Devices no longer need a data plane
Engineers no longer need to understand routing
questions.explanation: Controllers let you define policy once for the network and push consistent configuration to every device. Devices still need a data plane to forward traffic, and the knowledge to design and troubleshoot the network still matters.

questions.question: Which architecture centralizes the most control plane work in the controller?
choices: Cisco ACI with the APIC
Catalyst Center managing traditional switches
OpenFlow with an OpenDaylight controller
A traditional network running OSPF on every router
questions.explanation: In the OpenFlow model the controller computes and installs forwarding entries, leaving switches with mostly data plane work. ACI centralizes policy but leaves some control plane in the switches, and Catalyst Center managing traditional devices centralizes none of it.

questions.question: Catalyst Center manages a group of older switches using SSH and SNMP. What changes about how those switches build their routing and MAC tables?
choices: Nothing; they keep their own control plane, and the controller changes their configuration
The controller now computes every route and installs it directly
The switches stop running STP because the controller blocks ports itself
The switches send every frame to the controller for a forwarding decision
questions.explanation: Managing devices through the management plane does not move their control plane. The switches still run routing protocols, STP and MAC learning; the controller just configures and monitors them centrally.

questions.question: Which controller and southbound protocol go together in Cisco ACI?
choices: APIC with OpFlex
Catalyst Center with OpenFlow
OpenDaylight with OpFlex only
APIC with SNMP only
questions.explanation: ACI's controller is the Application Policy Infrastructure Controller (APIC), which pushes policy to the fabric switches with OpFlex. OpenFlow is the ONF's southbound protocol, used with controllers such as OpenDaylight.

questions.question: Catalyst Center goes offline for a planned upgrade. What happens to the campus network it manages?
choices: All traffic stops until the controller returns
Devices keep forwarding with their current configuration, but changes and the network-wide view are unavailable
Devices revert to their factory default configuration
Devices switch to OpenFlow and wait for a backup controller
questions.explanation: Catalyst Center is not in the forwarding path. Devices keep their configuration and tables and keep forwarding; you lose the ability to make changes, run assurance and use its API until it is back. That is why controllers are still deployed in highly available clusters.

questions.question: Which interface does an SDN controller use to program and configure the network devices below it?
choices: The northbound interface
The southbound interface
The management VLAN
The console port
questions.explanation: The southbound interface faces down to the devices. The northbound interface faces up to applications and scripts that use the controller.

questions.question: Which three are southbound protocols or APIs? Choose three.
choices: OpenFlow
OpFlex
NETCONF
The controller's REST API used by a Python script
JSON
questions.explanation: OpenFlow, OpFlex and NETCONF are used by controllers to talk down to devices. A script calling the controller's REST API is using the northbound interface, and JSON is a data format, not an interface.

questions.question: When a help desk ticket opens, the ticketing system asks Catalyst Center to run a path trace between the user's laptop and a server. Which statement is correct?
choices: The ticketing system uses the southbound API because the trace reaches the devices
The ticketing system needs SSH access to every switch on the path
The ticketing system uses the northbound REST API, and the controller gathers device data southbound
Path trace only works if every device on the path runs OpenFlow
questions.explanation: Applications talk to the controller northbound. The controller already collects configuration and forwarding data from devices through its southbound interfaces and does the path analysis itself, so the app never touches the switches.

questions.question: What transport and data encoding does NETCONF use?
choices: SSH with XML
HTTPS with JSON only
UDP with binary TLV fields
Telnet with plain CLI text
questions.explanation: NETCONF runs over SSH (port 830) and encodes data in XML, structured by YANG models. RESTCONF is the HTTPS-based alternative that can carry JSON or XML.

questions.question: Explain the difference between a northbound and a southbound API, with one example of each.
questions.answer: A northbound API faces up from the controller to applications and scripts, usually a REST API returning JSON, such as Catalyst Center's Intent API. A southbound API faces down to the devices, such as OpenFlow, OpFlex, NETCONF, RESTCONF, SSH or SNMP.
questions.explanation: Name the direction from the controller's point of view: up to the apps is north, down to the devices is south.

questions.question: In Cisco SD-Access, what is the overlay?
choices: The physical switches and links that provide IP reachability
Virtual networks carried in VXLAN tunnels between fabric nodes
The Catalyst Center GUI and its dashboards
The ISE database of users and groups
questions.explanation: The overlay is the set of virtual networks built on top of the underlay with VXLAN tunnels. The physical network and its routing are the underlay.

questions.question: Match each SD-Access component to its job.

pairs.right: Overlay data plane: encapsulates endpoint frames
Overlay control plane: maps endpoint IDs to locators
Routing protocol of a greenfield underlay
Group label used to enforce policy
Connects the fabric to outside networks

questions.explanation: VXLAN carries traffic and LISP tells nodes where endpoints are. IS-IS gives the routed underlay reachability, SGTs carry group membership for policy, and border nodes connect the fabric to the WAN or data center.

questions.question: An SD-Access edge node sends this packet into the fabric. Which statement is correct?
choices: Underlay switches route it using 10.1.3.1, the destination endpoint's address
172.16.3.3 is the destination endpoint's default gateway in the overlay
172.16.3.3 is the RLOC of the egress edge node, and the underlay routes on the outer header
The first underlay switch removes the inner header
questions.explanation: The ingress edge node addressed the outer header to the egress node's routing locator, learned from LISP. Underlay switches only look at that outer header; the egress edge node removes the VXLAN wrapper and delivers the original frame to 10.1.3.1.

questions.question: Put the SD-Access steps in order for the first frame sent to a new destination.
items: The egress edge node registers the destination's EID and its own RLOC with the LISP map server
A frame for that destination arrives at the ingress edge node
The ingress edge node asks the LISP mapping system where the destination EID lives
The ingress edge node learns the egress node's RLOC
The ingress node wraps the original frame in VXLAN with an outer IP header to that RLOC
The egress edge node removes the VXLAN wrapper and delivers the original frame
questions.explanation: Registration happens first, so the mapping system can answer. The ingress node then resolves the EID to an RLOC (LISP, control plane) and tunnels the frame there (VXLAN, data plane), and the egress node decapsulates it.

questions.question: A greenfield SD-Access fabric was built by Catalyst Center. Why is neither HSRP nor STP blocking needed between its access and distribution switches?
choices: All inter-switch links are routed Layer 3 links running IS-IS, and the edge node is the hosts' default gateway
Catalyst Center runs STP centrally and pushes the blocked ports to each switch
VXLAN replaces IP routing in the underlay
Each endpoint uses the LISP map server as its default gateway
questions.explanation: The routed access underlay has no Layer 2 links between switches, so there are no Layer 2 loops for STP to break, and IS-IS picks paths. With the gateway on the edge node itself, there is no pair of distribution gateways to make redundant with an FHRP.

questions.question: What does intent-based networking mean?
choices: Engineers write every device command, and the controller only stores backups
Devices guess the engineer's intent from traffic patterns, with no configuration
Policies are written as ACL lines on each interface
The engineer states the desired outcome, and the controller turns it into device configuration and checks the result
questions.explanation: With IBN you describe what should happen (for example, which groups may communicate). The controller works out and deploys the per-device configuration, then verifies the network behaves as intended.

questions.question: Which two network management tasks are performed by both traditional management platforms and Catalyst Center? Choose two.
choices: Discovering devices and building a topology map
Building and controlling an SD-Access fabric
Day 0 installation, day 1 configuration and day n monitoring
Enforcing scalable group tag policy across a fabric
questions.explanation: Discovery, topology maps and lifecycle management are traditional management features that Catalyst Center also has. SD-Access and SGT-based policy are what only Catalyst Center adds.

questions.question: An engineer must remove a security rule added two years ago for a project that has ended. Why is this easier with SD-Access group-based policy than with a long traditional ACL?
choices: Group policies are stored in every switch's startup-config
SD-Access never allows traffic to be denied
Catalyst Center deletes any rule older than one year
Each group policy is a separate entry, so one can be removed without affecting the others
questions.explanation: In a long ACL, one line may serve several old requirements and order matters, so removing it is risky. Group-based policies are kept separately per source and destination group, with notes, and can be removed independently.

questions.question: In 2023 Cisco renamed DNA Center. What is its current name?
questions.explanation: Cisco DNA Center became Cisco Catalyst Center in 2023. Older books, labs and exam questions still use the DNA Center name.

questions.question: In a cloud-managed network, which traffic goes to the vendor's cloud?
choices: All user traffic, so the cloud can inspect it
Only traffic headed to the internet
Only management traffic such as configuration, firmware and telemetry
No traffic; the dashboard polls devices with SNMP from inside your LAN
questions.explanation: Cloud management moves the management plane to the vendor's cloud. User traffic is still switched and routed locally by the devices on site.

questions.question: A new access point for a cloud-managed store is shipped straight to the store. What lets it configure itself when it is plugged in?
choices: Zero-touch provisioning: it contacts the cloud dashboard, which already knows its serial number and site
The store manager types the configuration at the console port
It copies its configuration from the nearest access point over Wi-Fi
An engineer must SSH to it from headquarters first
questions.explanation: Devices are claimed into the organization by serial or order number ahead of time. When the new device reaches the internet it contacts the cloud and downloads its configuration with no on-site expertise.

questions.question: Which is a real trade-off of cloud-managed networking?
choices: All user traffic gains latency because it passes through the cloud
Management depends on internet access to the vendor's cloud, and licensing is an ongoing subscription
Devices cannot be managed through any API
Every site needs its own on-premises controller
questions.explanation: You trade owning a controller for depending on the vendor's service: management needs internet access, licenses must stay current, and data about your network is held by a third party. User traffic stays local, and cloud dashboards have REST APIs.

questions.question: Which two are operational network management tasks rather than configuration management tasks? Choose two.
choices: Checking that every switch runs an approved, unmodified software image
Pushing a new ACL line to 300 branch routers
Alerting when an uplink's utilization keeps climbing week after week
Building access switch configurations from a template
Changing the SNMP community on every device
questions.explanation: Operational management watches the network: inventory, health, alerts, reports and image compliance. Pushing ACL lines, rendering templates and changing SNMP settings all change device configuration, which is configuration management.

questions.question: A configuration management tool compares SW7 with the standard for its role. What should it report?
questions.code:
! Standard for access switches
ntp server 10.0.0.10
logging host 10.0.0.20
snmp-server community R3adOnly RO
spanning-tree mode rapid-pvst

! SW7 running-config (matching section)
ntp server 10.0.0.9
logging host 10.0.0.20
snmp-server community R3adOnly RO
snmp-server community T3mpFix RW
spanning-tree mode rapid-pvst
choices: SW7 matches the standard; small differences in values are ignored
SW7 drifted only in its NTP server, because extra lines are never reported
SW7 has drifted: it uses an old NTP server and has an extra read-write SNMP community, probably left from a one-off fix
SW7's startup-config is out of date and needs copy running-config startup-config
questions.explanation: Drift is any difference from the intended configuration for the role. SW7 points to 10.0.0.9 instead of 10.0.0.10 and has an RW community the standard does not include, which is a security hole as well as drift. Good tools report missing lines and extra lines; one that ignored extras would miss exactly this kind of leftover emergency change.

questions.question: Put the stages of a managed switch's life in order.
items: Onboard the new switch, for example with Plug and Play
Apply the standard configuration for its role
Monitor, patch and change it for years
Decommission it and remove it from inventory
questions.explanation: Day 0 gets a device onto the network and under management, day 1 makes it do its job, and day n is everything after that until it is retired. Automation and controllers help at every stage.

questions.question: Which is a genuine trade-off of moving to a controller-based network?
choices: User traffic must pass through the controller, adding latency
The controller becomes critical infrastructure that must be highly available, secured and kept licensed
Devices can no longer be reached with SSH
Routing protocols stop running on every device
questions.explanation: Controllers are not in the forwarding path, so they add no latency to user traffic, and devices keep SSH and, in most designs, their routing protocols. The real costs are a controller that must be clustered, protected and licensed, and new skills for the team.

questions.question: Which statement about a single-site Cisco ACI spine-leaf fabric is correct?
choices: Servers connect to spine switches so they are one hop from everything
Leaf switches link directly to each other for redundancy
Spine switches form a full mesh with each other
Every leaf connects to every spine, and endpoints connect only to leaf switches
questions.explanation: In spine-leaf, each leaf has links to every spine, there are no leaf-to-leaf or spine-to-spine links, and all endpoints, including servers, the APIC and WAN routers, attach to leaves. Traffic between endpoints on different leaves always goes leaf, spine, leaf.

questions.question: Match each Cisco ACI term to its role.

pairs.right: Controller that turns policy into switch configuration
Set of endpoints that share the same policy
Southbound protocol that carries policy to the switches
Where servers, VMs and outside routers attach
Interconnects all the leaf switches

questions.explanation: The APIC holds the intent (EPGs and the policies between them) and pushes it to the Nexus switches with OpFlex. Endpoints attach to leaves, and spines only interconnect leaves.

questions.question: In an ACI data center, the virtualization platform moves a VM in the Web endpoint group to a server attached to a different leaf switch. What must the network engineer configure so the web policy keeps working?
choices: The access VLAN and an ACL on the new leaf port
A new EPG for the new leaf switch
Nothing; the VM stays in the Web EPG, and the APIC applies that EPG's policy wherever the VM now connects
A static route on each spine pointing to the VM
questions.explanation: ACI attaches policy to the EPG, not to ports or IP addresses. The APIC learns where the endpoint now is and programs the leaf it needs, so the policy follows the VM. Per-port VLANs and ACLs are the traditional model ACI replaces.

questions.question: What is YANG?
choices: A transport protocol that carries XML over SSH
A data modeling language that defines the structure and types of configuration and state data
Cisco's northbound REST API for Catalyst Center
An encryption method used by RESTCONF
questions.explanation: YANG defines what data exists, with names, types and structure. NETCONF and RESTCONF are the protocols that carry YANG-modeled data; NETCONF is the one that uses XML over SSH.

questions.question: Type the IOS XE global configuration command that enables the NETCONF server, so a controller or tool can manage the router with YANG models.
questions.explanation: netconf-yang starts the NETCONF agent, which listens over SSH on TCP port 830. RESTCONF is enabled separately with restconf, together with ip http secure-server.

questions.question: Match each southbound technology to its description.

pairs.right: XML-encoded operations over SSH on port 830
REST-style HTTPS URIs carrying JSON or XML
Language that models the data both of them carry
Writes match and action entries into switch flow tables

questions.explanation: NETCONF and RESTCONF are two transports for YANG-modeled data: XML over SSH, and HTTPS with JSON or XML. YANG itself is the modeling language, not a protocol. OpenFlow programs forwarding entries directly, the most centralized model.

questions.question: In Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN, which component is the management plane, providing the GUI, templates and northbound REST API?
choices: SD-WAN Validator (vBond)
SD-WAN Controller (vSmart)
SD-WAN Manager (vManage)
A WAN Edge router
questions.explanation: SD-WAN Manager is where engineers build templates and policy and monitor the WAN, and it exposes the REST API. The Controller runs OMP (control plane), the Validator onboards routers, and edge routers forward traffic.

questions.question: Match each Cisco SD-WAN component to the plane it provides.

pairs.right: Management plane: GUI, templates and monitoring
Control plane: routes and policy through OMP
Orchestration plane: authenticates and onboards routers
Data plane: forwards traffic through IPsec tunnels

questions.explanation: Cisco SD-WAN splits the planes across separate components. Only the edge routers carry user traffic; the other three manage, control and onboard them.

questions.question: A branch edge router reports these tunnel measurements. The video policy requires latency under 100 ms, loss under 2% and jitter under 20 ms. Which tunnel does application-aware routing use for video?
choices: MPLS, because MPLS is always preferred for real-time traffic
Internet, because it is the only tunnel that meets every part of the SLA
LTE, because it has the lowest loss of the two internet-based paths
None; video is dropped until MPLS recovers
questions.explanation: MPLS fails the latency limit (118 ms) and LTE fails the jitter limit (27 ms). The internet tunnel meets all three thresholds, so video uses it, still encrypted inside IPsec. Application-aware routing follows measured performance, not the reputation of the transport.

questions.question: For 20 minutes every branch loses contact with the SD-WAN Manager and Controllers, but the branches can still reach each other over the internet. What happens to traffic between two branches?
choices: It stops, because edge routers need the Controller to forward each packet
It is sent through the SD-WAN Manager, which takes over forwarding
The edge routers reboot and wait for zero-touch provisioning
It keeps flowing over the existing IPsec tunnels, using the routes and policy last received, for a graceful restart period
questions.explanation: The controllers provide the control and management planes only. Edge routers keep the OMP routes and keys they last learned and keep forwarding through existing tunnels for a graceful restart period. What you lose is the ability to change policy, onboard routers and see the network.

questions.question: In an SD-WAN, which part is the underlay?
choices: The MPLS, broadband and cellular networks that give the edge routers IP reachability to each other
The IPsec tunnels between the edge routers
The OMP sessions between the edge routers and the SD-WAN Controller
The application-aware routing policy
questions.explanation: The underlay is the transport that moves packets between sites. The IPsec tunnels built across it are the overlay, and OMP and policy belong to the control plane that runs the overlay.
